< # Session transcript: NVL72 inference animation and AWS deployment
< 
< Repository: `yosyp/llm-viz`
< 
< This file has the user's messages verbatim, Claude's final replies verbatim, and a condensed log of the work done in between. Raw tool output and screenshots are left out.

< 
< ## Turn 1
< 
< ### User
< 
< > create a self contained aesthetically pleasing, breathtaking animation of an nlv72 rack serving inference on a large model spanning multiple gpus like a kimi k3 or glm. Start with a view of the rack and then zoom into it to show inter gpu comms then inside one gpu, then going into the conceptual visualization of refill and decode and how multiple layers in the neural network and connected and then to the transformer and next token prediction, and finally into the single matmul that is taking place and break down that matmul into a series of multiplications.
< >
< > use javascript for it. be detailed and scientifically accurate. it should evoke awe.
< 
< ### Work log
< 
< - Found an empty repository on branch `claude/nlv72-inference-animation-5c2ob4`.
< - Wrote `nvl72-inference/index.html`, a single-file Canvas 2D animation with no dependencies:
<   - A timeline engine with 9 scenes. Transitions zoom through a focus point, so each scene first appears nested inside the one before it.
<   - Captions timed to the animation, a chapter progress bar, and keyboard controls. The URL takes `?s=`, `?t=` and `?pause`.
<   - The model is Kimi K2-class, using its published architecture: 61 layers, d = 7168, 64 MLA heads, 384 experts with top-8 routing plus 1 shared expert, and a 163,840-token vocabulary.
<   - The hardware figures are GB200 NVL72 and B200 specs.
< - Rendered screenshots across the whole timeline with Playwright and headless Chromium, and got no console errors.
< - Fixed the problems the screenshots showed:
<   - Text in the diagram scenes was too small, so each scene now has its own fit and a font scale.
<   - Text measurement ignored the font scale, which made "Sunlight" and "scatters" overlap.
<   - The logits were too flat.
<   - The FP8 bit readout overlapped other text in chapter 9.
<   - Callout labels needed a dark backing, and some had to fade out before the zoom transitions.
<   - Added a "rotate to landscape" hint for portrait phones.
< - Added `README.md`, committed, and pushed.
< - Could not open a PR, because the pushed branch was the repo's only branch.
< 
< ### Claude
< 
< I built the animation. It's a single self-contained file, `nvl72-inference/index.html`: plain JavaScript on Canvas, no dependencies, no build step. Open it in any modern browser. It plays about 3 minutes across 9 chapters and loops. Each chapter zooms into a point in the previous one, so every scene first appears nested inside the one before it.
< 
< I checked every chapter and the transitions between them in headless Chromium, with no console errors. I have only reviewed it as still frames, not watched it play in real time, so pacing and smoothness still need a live look.
< 
< **The chapters:**
< 1. **The rack:** a 3D row of racks with the NVL72 in the middle. You see compute trays whose GPU lights pulse, NVLink switch trays, the copper NVLink spine through the glass side panel, and the cooling pipes. The camera pushes in slowly.
< 2. **NVLink fabric:** 72 GPUs and 18 NVSwitch chips with all 1,296 links drawn. Each GPU hosts 6 experts, and hundreds of particles show the dispatch → expert → combine exchange at each MoE layer.
< 3. **One Blackwell GPU:** two dies joined by the 10 TB/s die-to-die link, 8 HBM3e stacks, and 148 working SMs (some drawn fused off for yield). Data streams from memory to L2 to the SMs, then one SM opens up to show its Tensor Cores and on-chip memories.
< 4. **Prefill and decode:** prefill processes the whole prompt at once; decode produces one token per step while re-reading the weights every step. The KV cache is handed from one to the other, and a roofline chart shows decode climbing as the batch grows.
< 5. **Through the layers:** an isometric tower of 61 layers. The token's hidden state rises through it, and each layer lights its router's 8 of 384 experts plus the shared one. Layer 1 is correctly shown as dense.
< 6. **Inside one layer:** attention with its compressed (latent) KV cache and causal attention heatmap, then the router's 384 scores and 9 expert SwiGLU MLPs, each added back into the residual stream.
< 7. **Next-token prediction:** the output head produces logits over 163,840 tokens, softmax turns them into probabilities, and a sampling needle picks a token. It builds "Sunlight scatters off air molecules, and blue light…", and one step deliberately picks the second-most-likely token.
< 8. **One matmul:** X (128×7168) times W (7168×2048), split into 128×128 tiles across SMs and walked 56 steps along the shared dimension, with the memory pipeline drawn below.
< 9. **Multiply, add, repeat:** one output number computed from 7,168 pairs of genuine 8-bit floats, shown bit by bit and summed at 32-bit precision. It starts slowly, speeds up to all 7,168, then ends on the totals up to rack scale and "Multiply. Add. Repeat."
< 
< **On accuracy:** I used the published Kimi K2 architecture as the model. I don't have public specs for Kimi K3, so the on-screen text says "Kimi K2-class, similar to GLM". The hardware figures are GB200 NVL72 and B200 specs. The tray order, cable routing, SM layout, the 128-token batch per expert and the example sentence are illustrative, and the README says so.
< 
< **Controls:** Space to pause, ←/→ to change chapter, R to restart, and click the progress bar to seek. Adding `?s=5` to the URL starts at chapter 5.
< 
< **Git:** the work is committed and pushed to `claude/nlv72-inference-animation-5c2ob4`, along with a README. I'll keep this small: one "For scale" card per comparison. It fades in beside the captions when the narrator reaches the number and fades out after about ten seconds, in the full walkthrough only. The comparisons, with the arithmetic checked:

  • 13.5 TB: the Apollo Guidance Computer had ~4 KB of working memory, so 13.5 TB ÷ 4 KB ≈ 3.3 billion of them.
  • 720 PFLOPS: if 8 billion people each did one calculation per second, 7.2×10¹⁷ ÷ 8×10⁹ ≈ 9×10⁷ s, which is about 3 years to match one second of the rack.
  • 120 kW: an average US home draws ~1.2 kW (≈10,500 kWh a year), so this is about 100 homes.
  • 3 km: the Eiffel Tower is 330 m, so the cables would stand about 9 Eiffel Towers tall.
  • 130 TB/s: an HD movie is ~5 GB, so that's ~26,000 movies a second. An HD stream is ~5 Mb/s, so it's also ~200 million HD streams at once.
  • 208 billion transistors: the IBM PC's Intel 8088 had 29,000, so one GPU equals about 7 million of those chips.
